narrative:
This swing trading run looked at two large healthcare companies: UnitedHealth Group (UNH) and Johnson & Johnson (JNJ). Swing trading means trying to capture price moves that play out over 2–20 trading days — not day trading, and not long-term investing. You set an entry price, a target where you take profit, and a stop-loss level where you cut your loss if the trade goes against you.

For UNH, the story is dramatic but frustrating: the stock has been on a rocket ship. It surged more than 34% in just 21 trading days — an extraordinary move. The trend is undeniably real, with every technical indicator screaming momentum. But here is the problem: the stock is so stretched above its normal moving averages (think of a moving average as the stock's 'average path' over time) that there is no safe entry point in either direction. Buying now would mean chasing a stock at peak extension. Shorting (betting it will fall) is also dangerous because a trend this powerful can keep running far longer than any short-seller can survive. One agent — the mean reversion specialist — made a reasonable case for a bearish fade, pointing to an RSI (a momentum gauge where above 70 is 'overbought') of 94.45, which is an extreme reading. But four out of five strategy agents said no: with ADX (a trend strength measure) at 85.61, one of the highest readings possible, fighting this trend directly is asking to get steamrolled. The system's verdict: wait patiently for UNH to pull back to its 10-day moving average around $348–$355 before considering any trade.

For JNJ, the picture is clearer and already in motion. Four out of five swing strategies agreed: JNJ is in a confirmed downtrend, underperforming while the broader market hit all-time highs. The EMA stack (a cascade of moving averages — when they line up in a staircase pointing downward, that confirms a bearish trend) is fully bearish. Momentum in every timeframe is negative. Crucially, the portfolio already holds a short position in JNJ — 3 shares entered at $229.06, now sitting at $224.07 with roughly $14.85 in unrealized profit. The measured-move target (a calculation based on the height of the price range JNJ broke out of) sits at $216.53, still about $7.50 below current price. The system's job now is not to add more exposure, but to hold the existing position and let it run to target. The stop-loss remains at $231.50 — if JNJ bounces back above that level, the trade would be exited at a modest loss.

The main tensions in this run: UNH created real disagreement between the mean-reversion agent (who wanted to short the extreme) and everyone else (who said the trend is too strong to fade). For JNJ, there was no directional disagreement — all four bearish agents agreed on direction — but they diverged on the ideal entry level, ranging from $223.50 to $229. Since the position is already in flight at a good entry, this disagreement is academic. The portfolio context — already running balanced positions in BAC (long), DIS (long), AAPL (long), AMD (short), META (short), and JNJ (short) — meant no new positions were warranted anyway. The risk manager confirmed the position limits were already at capacity for JNJ.

concepts.Swing Trading: Swing trading is a style of trading where you hold positions for 2–20 days to capture a medium-term price move. It is longer than day trading (which ends each day) but shorter than investing (which can last years). You pick a direction, set a specific entry price, a profit target, and a stop-loss level, then let the trade play out over days or weeks.
concepts.Entry Price: The entry price is your buy (or sell) alarm — the specific price at which you want to open a trade. Think of it as your trigger point. Setting an entry in advance, rather than just buying at the current price, helps you get a better position and avoid chasing moves.
concepts.Target Price: The target price is where you plan to take your profit and close the trade. If you buy a stock at $100 and your target is $115, you are aiming for a 15% gain. You set this in advance so you are not tempted to get greedy and overstay your welcome.
concepts.Stop-Loss: A stop-loss is the price level where you will exit the trade to cut your losses. If you buy at $100 and set a stop at $95, you are saying: 'If this trade goes wrong and the stock falls to $95, I'm out and I accept a 5% loss.' It prevents a small loss from becoming a devastating one.
concepts.Risk-Reward Ratio: The risk-reward ratio compares how much you could gain versus how much you could lose on a trade. A 3:1 ratio means for every $1 you risk losing, you could gain $3. Swing traders typically require at least 2:1 to take a trade — you want the potential upside to be at least twice the downside.
concepts.Short Selling: Shorting a stock is a way to profit when a stock falls. You borrow shares and sell them at today's price, then later buy them back at a lower price and return them — pocketing the difference. If the stock rises instead, you lose money. It is the reverse of normal investing.
concepts.Hold: In this context, 'hold' means no new trade action — either because you already have a position you are letting run, or because there is no good entry setup and you are waiting on the sidelines.
concepts.RSI (Relative Strength Index): RSI measures how fast and how much a stock has moved recently, on a scale from 0 to 100. Above 70 means the stock may be 'overbought' (risen too fast, due for a rest). Below 30 means 'oversold' (fallen too fast, possibly due for a bounce). It does not predict direction on its own but flags extremes where reversals are more likely.
concepts.ADX (Average Directional Index): ADX measures how strong a trend is, regardless of whether it is up or down. Below 20 = no clear trend (choppy). 20–50 = moderate trend. 50+ = strong trend. 80+ = extreme, almost parabolic trend. High ADX tells you the trend is real and powerful; it does not tell you which direction.
concepts.EMA (Exponential Moving Average): An EMA is a moving average that gives more weight to recent prices. The 10-day EMA reacts quickly to price changes; the 50-day EMA moves slowly and shows the longer-term trend. When short-term EMAs are above longer-term ones, it signals an uptrend (and vice versa for downtrends). A 'death stack' is when all EMAs line up bearishly.
concepts.MACD (Moving Average Convergence Diverge: MACD is a momentum indicator that shows the relationship between two moving averages. When the MACD line crosses below its signal line, or when the histogram (the bar chart showing the gap between the two lines) turns negative, it signals building selling pressure. Traders use it to time entries and exits.
concepts.Bollinger Bands: Bollinger Bands are three lines plotted on a price chart: a middle line (the 20-day moving average) and two outer bands that represent statistical price boundaries. When bands are 'tight' (close together), the stock is coiling — a big move is coming but direction is unknown. When price is near the lower band, it is at a short-term extreme low; near the upper band means short-term extreme high.
concepts.Z-Score: A z-score measures how far away something is from its average, in units of standard deviations. A z-score of +2 means the price is 2 standard deviations above its average — statistically, this happens only about 5% of the time. Z-scores above +2 or below -2 flag unusual extremes that often revert toward the mean.
concepts.Measured Move: A measured move is a price target calculated by taking the height of a price range and projecting it beyond a breakout or breakdown point. Example: if a stock consolidates between $230 and $223.78 (a range of $6.22), and then breaks below $223.78, the measured-move target is $223.78 - $6.22 = $217.56. It is a widely used technical method for setting targets.
concepts.Support Level: A support level is a price where the stock has repeatedly stopped falling and bounced back up — like a floor the market keeps defending. The more times a price level holds, the more significant it becomes. When support finally breaks, it often becomes resistance (the former floor becomes a ceiling).
concepts.Resistance Level: A resistance level is a price where the stock has repeatedly stopped rising and pulled back — like a ceiling the market keeps running into. Resistance that is repeatedly tested and then finally broken can become new support.
concepts.OBV (On-Balance Volume): OBV is a volume indicator that adds volume on up days and subtracts it on down days, creating a running total. When OBV is trending down while price is flat or rising, it means institutional investors are quietly selling into the rally — a bearish divergence warning.
concepts.Parabolic Move: A parabolic move is when a stock's price chart starts to curve upward at an accelerating angle — like a hockey stick — rather than rising steadily. These moves are exciting when they happen but historically end with sharp reversals, because the stock has risen far faster than any fundamentals can justify.
concepts.Oversold: Oversold means a stock has fallen so much, so quickly, that a short-term bounce is statistically likely. It does NOT mean the long-term trend has changed. A stock can be oversold in a downtrend — it may bounce briefly, then resume falling. RSI below 30 is the common oversold threshold.
concepts.Dead-Cat Bounce: A dead-cat bounce is a brief, temporary recovery in a stock that is otherwise in a downtrend. The name comes from the morbid idea that even a dead cat will bounce if it falls from high enough. These bounces can fool investors into thinking the decline is over, but the downtrend then resumes.
concepts.Short Cover / Short-Covering Rally: When people who have shorted a stock all rush to buy back their shares at the same time (to close their positions and cut losses), this creates sudden upward buying pressure — a 'short-covering rally.' These can be sharp and fast, which is why short sellers use stop-losses.
